verses.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning Yahweh’s name, she came to test him with hard questions.

She came to Jerusalem with a very great caravan, with camels that bore spices, very much gold, and precious stones; and when she had come to Solomon, she talked with him about all that was in her heart.
Solomon answered all her questions. There was not anything hidden from the king which he didn’t tell her.
When the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,

the food of his table, the sitting of his servants, the attendance of his officials, their clothing, his cup bearers, and his ascent by which he went up to Yahweh’s house; there was no more spirit in her.
She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts, and of your wisdom.
However I didn’t believe the words until I came and my eyes had seen it. Behold, not even half was told me! Your wisdom and prosperity exceed the fame which I heard.
Happy are your men, happy are these your servants, who stand continually before you, who hear your wisdom.
Blessed is Yahweh your God, who delighted in you, to set you on the throne of Israel. Because Yahweh loved Israel forever, therefore he made you king, to do justice and righteousness.”

She gave the king one hundred twenty talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. Never again was there such an abundance of spices as these which the queen of Sheba gave to king Solomon.
The fleet of Hiram that brought gold from Ophir, also brought in from Ophir great quantities of almug trees  and precious stones.
The king made of the almug trees pillars for Yahweh’s house, and for the king’s house, harps also and stringed instruments for the singers; no such almug trees came or were seen, to this day.
King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatever she asked, besides that which Solomon gave her of his royal bounty. So she turned and went to her own land, she and her servants.
Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents  of gold,
besides that which the traders brought, and the traffic of the merchants, and of all the kings of the mixed people, and of the governors of the country.
King Solomon made two hundred bucklers of beaten gold; six hundred shekels  of gold went to one buckler.
he made three hundred shields of beaten gold; three minas  of gold went to one shield; and the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with the finest gold.
There were six steps to the throne, and the top of the throne was round behind; and there were armrests on either side by the place of the seat, and two lions standing beside the armrests.
Twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other on the six steps. Nothing like it was made in any kingdom.

All king Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. None were of silver, because it was considered of little value in the days of Solomon.
For the king had a fleet of Tarshish at sea with Hiram’s fleet. Once every three years the fleet of Tarshish came, bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
So king Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.
All the earth sought the presence of Solomon, to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart.
Year after year, every man brought his tribute, vessels of silver, vessels of gold, clothing, armor, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had one thousand four hundred chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, that he kept in the chariot cities and with the king at Jerusalem.
The king made silver as common as stones in Jerusalem, and cedars as common as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland.
The horses which Solomon had were brought out of Egypt. The king’s merchants received them in droves, each drove at a price.

A chariot came up and went out of Egypt for six hundred shekels  of silver, and a horse for one hundred fifty shekels; and so they exported them to all the kings of the Hittites, and to the kings of Syria.

footnotes.content: Fame of the Lord's name travels farther than we know. The queen of Sheba, ruling a distant kingdom, heard of Solomon's wisdom and came to see for herself—not to worship, but to test him. Sometimes the Lord works through our reputation to draw searching hearts close.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A caravan laden with spices, gold, and precious stones—goods from the great trade routes of the ancient world. She came not as a casual visitor but with the weight and dignity of her throne. She brought the best her kingdom could offer, a sign of respect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon didn't dodge her questions or speak around them. Wisdom opens the mouth to speak truth plainly. His answers came from a heart that sought to serve, and the Lord gave him words that satisfied her searching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She moved through his house, seeing the visible fruit of his reign—the order, the craft, the abundance. Wisdom isn't only in words; it shows in how we build, arrange, and care for what we're given.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The grandeur overwhelmed her. His table, his servants standing ready, the routes by which he climbed to worship—all spoke of a life ordered toward justice and the Lord. Her spirit was silent, which means she finally saw something true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She begins to speak from her heart, not to test anymore. What she'd heard in her own land turned out to be true. I've learned that when we encounter real faithfulness and genuine wisdom, we can't help but acknowledge it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Not even half was told me." The reality exceeded the report. Her own eyes, her own presence in his house, showed her more than any messenger could have conveyed. Sometimes you have to see a faithful life with your own eyes to believe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She noticed the happiness of those who serve him. A good ruler doesn't crush his people but makes them glad to stand before him. That kind of joy in service is rare and tells you something true about a man's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From a foreign queen comes a blessing: "Blessed is Yahweh your God." She recognizes that Solomon's throne, his wisdom, his justice—all come from the Lord's hand. The Lord loves Israel, and so He placed Solomon there to rule with righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One hundred twenty talents of gold and spices so rare they'd never come again in such abundance. Her gift was immense, a token of honor. In the ancient world, such treasures sealed respect between rulers and opened pathways for future peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hiram's ships brought almug trees and precious stones from Ophir—a legendary source of wealth in that age. Trade routes connected distant peoples and brought rare materials that showed a nation's reach and prosperity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The almug wood became pillars for the Lord's house, and harps for worship. Solomon took the treasures the Lord gave him and turned them toward the Lord's glory. He used his wealth not for himself alone, but to beautify worship.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon gave her all she desired—more than any king had to spare. She came searching, found wisdom and hospitality, and returned home honored. His generosity matched his wisdom; both flowed from a heart aware of the Lord's gift.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six hundred sixty-six talents of gold came to him year after year. The numbers are staggering. Yet even abundance can become a snare if we forget it comes from the Lord's hand and that we hold it only for a season.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The gold flowed in from trade, merchants, tributary kings—from every direction, blessing poured into Jerusalem. Solomon's kingdom was a hub where commerce and tribute converged, reflecting his fame and the stability his wisdom brought.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two hundred shields of beaten gold, six hundred shekels each. These weren't mere ornaments; they were the defensive armor of a king at the height of power. Gold shields proclaimed wealth, but also readiness to defend his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hundred more shields of beaten gold, stored in the House of the Forest of Lebanon—a fortress built with cedarwood. The arsenal itself was a marvel, showing how Solomon prepared his kingdom not with pomp alone but with substance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A throne of ivory overlaid with finest gold—a seat of judgment and authority. The craftsmen who made it understood that power in the eyes of people is partly how it appears, but the true throne belongs to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six steps led up to it, with a rounded back and armrests, flanked by lions standing guard. The design spoke of majesty and ascent—you climbed to reach the king's ear. In Solomon's age, such a throne showed the world that justice requires dignity and distance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twelve lions on the six steps, six on each side—a garrison of carved stone guarding the path to his seat. Nothing like it had been made anywhere. Yet all this artistry, all this gold and ivory—it was built by a man who believed it all belonged to the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every cup, every vessel in his house was gold. Silver, once precious, became common as dust. The abundance was complete, surrounding him. Yet I've learned that wealth like this can hide the loneliness of a heart that has forgotten why the Lord blessed it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fleet of Tarshish sailed the deep trade routes with Hiram's ships, returning once every three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. These exotic creatures and goods spoke of a kingdom connected to the far reaches of the known world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon surpassed every king in riches and wisdom. He had reached the peak. But I think of how often the greatest test comes not in climbing to the summit but in what we do when we find ourselves alone at the top.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the earth sought his presence to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. The world recognized that his understanding was no accident, but a gift from heaven. When the Lord gives wisdom, it shows—and draws others near.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Year by year, tributes arrived: vessels of silver and gold, fine clothing, armor, spices, horses, mules. The tribute never stopped because the world saw in Solomon a ruler blessed by heaven. Yet none of it could be taken with him when his days were done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen—a military machine unmatched in his day. He had gathered might that made him seem invincible on earth. But power, like gold, can slip through the fingers of a man who forgets his need for the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver became as common as stones in Jerusalem, and cedars as common as sycamore trees in the lowland. The precious became ordinary because there was so much of it. Sometimes abundance teaches us something hard: that enough never stays enough unless the heart learns to be grateful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's horses came from Egypt, brought by his merchants in droves. The trade in horses was lucrative and strategic—a nation's strength rode on its cavalry. Egypt's fine horses were prized throughout the ancient world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A chariot from Egypt cost six hundred shekels of silver; a horse, one hundred fifty shekels. Solomon became a middleman for other kings, buying and selling chariots and horses to the Hittites and Syria. Readers today hear an echo in this: even wisdom can slowly turn to commerce and profit-seeking, and we can drift from justice into mere dealing without noticing when it happened.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
